strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: using RL (GRPO) with an explicit efficiency reward (token reduction ratio) plus an accuracy reward to make a pretrained MLLM's token sparsity inference-consistent, rather than relying on post-hoc pruning heuristics or training-from-scratch sparse architectures.

Broad empirical coverage for a short paper: three Qwen2/2.5-VL models (3B/7B), 7 image and 6 video benchmarks evaluated with a standard harness (LMMs-Eval), showing a substantial token ratio reduction (~80% to ~23-25%) with only small accuracy changes.

The training setup (random threshold sampling p ~ U(0,1) within groups) is a sensible exploration mechanism for the efficiency-performance frontier, and the write-up of the sparse attention formulation is clear.
The method is post-training only and compatible with existing well-posed MLLMs, which is practically relevant for deployment.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially GRPO applied on top of ZipVL with a two-term reward (binary accuracy + 1 - token ratio). Both the sparse attention mechanism and the RL algorithm are inherited; the contribution is the reward design, which is quite simple. The paper does not clearly delineate what is non-trivial beyond tuning ZipVL's operating point.

No actual efficiency measurements: the central claim of 'alleviating computation and memory bottlenecks' and 'achievable inference-time acceleration' is supported only by the token ratio. There are no wall-clock latency, FLOPs, throughput, or KV-cache memory numbers, which are the metrics that matter for an acceleration paper.

Evaluation is potentially confounded: at inference, p is fixed at 0.975 for both ZipVL and ZipR1, yet ZipVL yields ~80% token ratio while ZipR1 yields ~23%. The mechanism by which RL updates on text tokens so drastically change ZipVL's dynamic ratio allocation is never explained or analyzed. Without this analysis, it is hard to verify the result is not an artifact of a changed operating regime.

Weak baselines: only Full attention and ZipVL are compared. Other training-free token pruning methods for MLLMs (e.g., FastV, SparseVLM, PyramidDrop, VisionZip) directly reduce tokens to 10-30% and should be included for a fair assessment of whether RL post-training adds value.

No ablations: the equal weighting of performance and efficiency rewards, the KL coefficient β, group size N, the U(0,1) threshold sampling scheme, the role of the Video-R1-260k calibration data, and sensitivity to the inference threshold p are all unexplored. Key hyperparameters and training cost are also unreported.

Small differences on many benchmarks (often within tenths of a point, and sometimes improvements after aggressive pruning) are reported without variance, seeds, or significance tests; 'minimal accuracy reduction' claims would benefit from repeated runs.

Writing and presentation issues: typos ('RL-baseed', 'directly optimize'), a low-resolution overview figure, and an unusually short experimental analysis section (one paragraph) leave important details about how the token ratio evolves during training unaddressed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: actively encouraging token sparsity in pretrained MLLMs via post-training is a relevant and under-explored direction, complementing inference-time token selection methods.
The core idea of treating token reduction ratio as an efficiency reward and answer accuracy as a performance reward within GRPO is simple, clean, and inference-consistent.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: three Qwen2/2.5-VL model sizes evaluated on 13 image and video benchmarks using the standard LMMs-Eval harness, with the headline claim (token ratio reduced from ~80% to ~25% with minimal accuracy loss) supported by the reported tables.
Building on ZipVL's Top-p sparse attention provides an existing, compatible mechanism through which the RL policy can modulate sparsity.
weaknesses: No actual efficiency measurements: despite the paper's central motivation being inference acceleration (computation and memory bottlenecks), it never reports wall-clock latency, throughput, FLOPs, or KV cache memory. Token ratio alone does not demonstrate realizable speedup, so the central efficiency claim is not validated.

Missing mechanism analysis: at inference both ZipVL and ZipR1 use the same fixed threshold p = 0.975, yet ZipR1 achieves a far lower token ratio. The paper never explains or analyzes how RL training changes the attention distribution to select fewer tokens at the same threshold, which is the crux of the method. Training curves and attention visualizations are absent.

Very limited baselines: the only comparison is against full attention and ZipVL. There is no comparison against the substantial body of visual token pruning/merging methods (e.g., FastV, VisionZip, SparseVLM, PyramidDrop) or other sparsity-inducing training approaches, making it impossible to judge whether RL-based post-training is actually the right tool versus simpler alternatives.

No ablations at all: no study of the reward weighting (fixed equal weights r_per + r_eff), the KL coefficient β, the number of sampled responses N, the uniform threshold sampling range, or the KL/self-distillation term the paper highlights as a key component.
The claimed benefit of 'flexibility with token reduction strength at inference time' is never evaluated; no accuracy-vs-ratio curves at different inference thresholds are provided.

Modest novelty: the method is essentially standard GRPO (DeepSeek-R1 style) applied on top of an existing sparse attention mechanism (ZipVL) with an added efficiency reward term; the technical contribution is thin for a top-tier venue.

Statistical rigor is lacking: all results appear to be single runs with no variance or significance analysis, and several ZipR1 numbers slightly exceed the full-attention baseline, suggesting noise rather than genuine improvements.
Reproducibility concerns: training details are sparse (no learning rate, batch size, number of GRPO steps, compute budget, or subset of Video-R1-260k actually used), and no code release is mentioned.

Presentation issues: several typos ('RL-baseed', 'directly optimize'), misuse of terminology (describing the KL-to-reference penalty as minimizing 'transfer entropy'), and a very short paper (~3 pages of content) with limited discussion, related work depth, and limitations section.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and practical: using RL (GRPO) with an efficiency reward (token reduction ratio) to actively encourage sparsity in an already-trained MLLM, rather than only passively exploiting existing attention sparsity. This is a sensible direction for post-training deployment scenarios.
Evaluation breadth is good: 13 image and video benchmarks spanning multiple capabilities, evaluated with the standard LMMs-Eval harness, across three model variants (Qwen2VL-7B, Qwen2.5VL-3B/7B).

The reported results are consistent and plausible: token ratio drops from ~70-80% (ZipVL) to ~22-24% with accuracy essentially preserved (and occasionally slightly improved), which, if correct, is a meaningful efficiency gain.

Building on Top-p sparse attention (ZipVL) with uniformly sampled thresholds p during rollouts is a simple, inference-consistent way to explore the efficiency-performance tradeoff, and the paper is generally easy to follow.
The method is post-training and model-agnostic in spirit, which increases its practical relevance.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is under-explained. The token budget tau is determined by Top-p selection over attention scores, and the threshold p is sampled uniformly rather than learned. The paper does not explain how the GRPO policy gradient (over output text tokens) actually propagates through the discrete, non-differentiable token-selection operation to concentrate attention and reduce tau. Without this, it is unclear whether the sparsification comes from RL at all versus simply tuning/calibrating ZipVL.

No wall-clock efficiency results. For a paper whose central claim is inference acceleration, reporting only the token ratio is insufficient; end-to-end prefill/decode latency, KV-cache memory, and throughput measurements are necessary to substantiate the 'acceleration' claim, since token ratio does not automatically translate to speedup with existing sparse kernels.

Weak baselines. The only sparsity baseline is ZipVL itself. There is no comparison against the many existing visual-token pruning/merging methods (e.g., FastV, SparseVLM, PyramidDrop, VTW) or other RL-based token-reduction approaches, making it hard to judge the contribution's competitiveness.

No ablations: the effect of the reward weighting (equal r_per + r_eff), the uniformly sampled threshold range, the KL coefficient beta, the number of rollouts N, and training compute/data details are all missing. The claim that 'p is set within [0.94, 0.975] with step 0.005' is stated but not analyzed.

Limited novelty beyond composition. The method is essentially ZipVL (existing sparse attention) + GRPO (existing algorithm) + a two-term reward. Related RL-based adaptive token/efficiency control for VLMs exists in the literature but is not discussed or differentiated.

Several technical statements are vague or questionable: the constraint in Eq. (3) is stated without derivation or discussion of how it relates to the actual Top-p selection; the claimed error bound (1-p) x ||V|| is borrowed without qualification; and terms like 'transfer entropy' (for KL to the reference model) are used loosely.

Reproducibility concerns: training hyperparameters (learning rate, steps, batch size, hardware, training cost), calibration data preprocessing, and code availability are not provided; no variance/seeds are reported despite small accuracy differences of 0.1-1 point being used to claim 'minimal reduction'.

The paper is very short (roughly 4 pages of content), with a thin method section and a single experiment section; analysis of failure cases, per-layer/per-task sparsity behavior, or generalization to other model families is absent.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: using GRPO with a joint correctness + token-reduction reward to actively enforce (rather than merely exploit) token sparsity in MLLMs is a sensible and relatively novel framing, and the paper is well positioned against both training-free sparse attention and trainable-sparse-attention/regularizer lines of work.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 13 image and video benchmarks across four MLLM backbones (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, LLaVA-Video-7B), with comparisons to FastV, VisionZip, ZipVL, MInference, MOBA, and a sharpness-loss baseline, plus budget-sweep curves (Fig. 3), runtime/memory measurements, and robustness analysis on HallusionBench.

Reported efficiency gains are practically meaningful: ~75% token reduction with near-baseline accuracy, up to 3.3x decoding speedup and 3x memory reduction at 200k sequence lengths, and the framework requires no architecture change or training from scratch.

Useful ablations: sparse attention mechanism choice (top-k vs. top-p vs. threshold), p-range and group-size sensitivity, layer-wise sparsity evolution (Fig. 5), and a clear discussion of why grouped-rollout RL is preferred over DPO-style preferences for a non-stationary trade-off frontier.
The reward design detail — gating the efficiency reward on group-level correctness (Eq. 8-9) to avoid collapsing to trivial ultra-sparse policies — shows thoughtful handling of a real failure mode.
weaknesses: Missing critical control experiment: the method conflates 'sparsity enforcement' with 'RL post-training for accuracy'. Sparsity Forcing at ~25% tokens often matches or exceeds the full-attention model (e.g., Qwen2-VL 70.8 vs 70.9; Qwen2.5-VL-7B avg 70.0 vs 70.2 in Table 3), suggesting much of the gain may come from RL on correctness rather than smarter sparsity. An ablation with GRPO + correctness reward only (no efficiency term, inference at standard budgets) is needed to attribute gains properly; without it, the central claim that RL 'reinforces' sparsity is under-supported.

Inconsistencies across tables undermine confidence in the numbers: Table 3 reports Full Qwen2.5-VL-7B ChartQA=84.0, MME=2303, VideoMME avg=64.5, while Table 1/Table 2 report values in the same ranges but Table 3's Sparsity Forcing avg (70.0) uses a different aggregation than Table 1 (73.6); the abstract's 'raises token reduction from 20% to 75%' phrasing is confusing (ratio vs. reduction) and is stated differently in Section 5 ('80% to 25%').

Train/inference mismatch in the core knob: training sweeps p in [0.94, 0.975] but inference fixes p=0.975; the mechanism by which multi-budget rollouts at high p alone yields 75% token reduction while fixed p=0.975 inference benefits is not clearly explained (the retained-token ratio at a given p is a property of attention distribution, not directly controllable by the threshold).

Equation 5 as written is ill-defined: 'p ∈ Z' collides with the retention threshold p ∈ [0,1] defined earlier, and the constraint 'sum of attention scores ≥ p × l' over a row-wise softmax needs clarification (per-row vs. aggregated), raising doubts about the formal correctness of the top-p budget derivation.

RL training cost and net efficiency are not accounted: multiple sequential rollouts per query with different KV-cache trajectories (admitted in Limitations) make training expensive (8 A100s); the paper does not report training cost or amortized analysis showing end-to-end (train + inference) efficiency benefit.
No statistical significance or variance reporting for any benchmark; several reported differences are within ~0.2-0.5 points, and LLaVA-Video results with MInference are within noise (61.3 vs 61.3).

Comparison fairness: MOBA and the sharpness-loss baselines are post-trained with a fixed 25% budget, whereas the method dynamically chooses budgets — the comparison would be stronger if baselines were swept across matched budgets or trained with the same RL budget-hint.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem: pushing token reduction in MLLMs beyond the ~50% plateau of training-free sparse attention methods.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 13 image and video benchmarks, 4 model backbones, multiple baseline families (training-free sparse attention, trainable sparse attention, sharpness-regularized post-training), plus ablations on sparse attention mechanisms, p-range, group size, and a hallucination robustness check.
The reported results are impressive if taken at face value: token ratios of ~25% with near-parity accuracy, 3.3× decoding speedup and 3× memory reduction at 200k sequence lengths.

The group-gated reward (Eq. 8-9), which disables the efficiency reward when no rollout in the group is correct, is a sensible design choice against collapse to trivial ultra-sparsity, and the discussion of why grouped-rollout RL fits this non-stationary trade-off is reasonable.
The paper is generally well written and the pipeline (training mirrors inference with pruning and KV-cache management) is clearly described.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially GRPO with a weighted sum of binary correctness and token-ratio rewards applied on top of an existing sparse attention mechanism (ZipVL) and an existing RL algorithm. The conceptual step from prior efficiency-reward RL work to this setting is incremental.

Unclear credit assignment: the paper never precisely specifies what the learnable policy actually controls. ZipVL's token selection is a deterministic function of the attention scores, and the threshold p is sampled from a fixed uniform distribution rather than being learned. The token ratio thus changes only indirectly through attention distribution sharpening, and the paper does not convincingly explain how the policy gradient is expected to reduce retained tokens. This weakens the core mechanistic claim.

Missing a crucial ablation: since inference simply fixes p at 0.975 (the upper bound of the training range), the gains may largely stem from attention sharpening during fine-tuning. A comparison against plain SFT-style post-training with the same data (or even the same reward under teacher forcing, which the paper dismisses on theoretical grounds but never tests empirically) is needed to substantiate the claim that RL is the right tool.

Attribution of gains is confounded: Table 3 baselines (MOBA at a fixed 25% budget, L∞ sharpness loss) appear implemented by the authors with somewhat ad hoc configurations, and fairness of these comparisons is questionable.

Reported differences over the full-attention baseline are often within noise (e.g., 70.8 vs 70.9, 73.6 vs 73.8), yet no variance estimates, seeds, or significance tests are provided; 'minimal accuracy decline' claims rest on single-run point estimates.

Efficiency comparisons (3.3× latency, 3× memory) are made only against dense FlashAttention-2, not against the strongest competing sparse methods at matched token ratios; end-to-end wall-clock comparisons to ZipVL/Minference are absent.

Several technical presentation issues: notation clash between threshold p in [0,1] and integer p in Eq. (5); the constrained-optimization formulation (Eq. 3) is stated but its connection to the actual top-p implementation is loose; the claim of a theoretical error bound (1-p)×|V| is cited rather than derived or validated.
Training cost of the method (sequential multi-budget rollouts, acknowledged in limitations) is not quantified, so the practical efficiency-per-training-FLOP trade-off cannot be judged.

No evaluation of potential side effects of full-model RL fine-tuning on general language/reasoning capabilities, only on the same multimodal benchmark family used for training distribution (Video-R1-260k).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: pushing sparse attention in MLLMs beyond the ~50% budget plateau that training-free methods reach, by actively enforcing sparsity rather than merely exploiting it.

Elegant and principled formulation: casting the efficiency-accuracy trade-off as a joint reward within GRPO, with the correctness-gated efficiency reward (Eq. 8-9) thoughtfully avoiding collapse to trivial ultra-sparse policies, and multi-budget rollouts providing a natural exploration mechanism for the minimal correctness-preserving budget.

Training/inference alignment is a genuinely valuable design choice: the same token pruning policy and KV-cache management used at deployment are used during RL training, addressing the known teacher-forcing mismatch of SFT-based sparsity methods.

Comprehensive empirical validation: 13 image/video benchmarks across three model families (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, LLaVA-Video-7B), consistent token ratio reductions (e.g., ZipVL 80%->25% on QwenVL) with near-baseline accuracy, plus HallusionBench robustness analysis and actual prefill latency/memory measurements (3.3x speedup, 3x memory reduction).

Useful ablations on sparse attention mechanism (top-k vs. threshold vs. top-p), p-range and group size, and informative qualitative analyses (layer-wise sparsity evolution in Fig. 5, budget scaling in Fig. 4b).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core contribution is an application of GRPO with an efficiency-augmented reward on top of an existing sparse attention mechanism (ZipVL). The algorithmic machinery is largely standard, and the sparse attention backbone itself is borrowed; the contribution is more of a well-executed post-training recipe than a new technique.

Indirect credit assignment concern: the sparse mask depends on the threshold p sampled uniformly, and RL gradients flow only through model weights, not through the mask selection itself. The paper does not deeply analyze whether the gains come from genuine learned sparsity policy vs. global attention sharpening, and how stable this is across seeds. No variance or statistical significance is reported for any benchmark results.

Comparison fairness in Table 3: baselines (MOBA, sharpness loss) are run at a fixed 25% budget while Sparsity Forcing selects 26.4% dynamically; a comparison at matched average ratios, and comparisons against other learned-pruning or RL-based efficiency methods, would strengthen the claim of superiority.

A gap between the framing and the inference configuration: training sweeps p in [0.94, 0.975] with multi-budget rollouts, yet at inference p is simply fixed at 0.975. This raises questions about how much of the multi-budget exploration is actually necessary, and the headline '75% token reduction' requires careful reading against the actual inference setup.

Some inconsistencies and clarity issues: Table 3 text reports 70.3 average vs. the table's 70.0 (and Full at 70.0 vs. 70.2 across text/table); the token budget formulation and the 'step size of 0.005' for p in training are under-specified; the constrained optimization in Eq. 3 motivates top-p masking but the exact relaxation is not derived.

Training cost of the method is high (sequential multi-budget rollouts, as acknowledged in limitations) and the cost/benefit trade-off versus simply tuning a fixed sparsity ratio per layer (which Fig. 5 suggests matters) is not quantified. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many implementation details involved.
